Maven versions with Maven's rules instead of guessing (#124)

* order Maven versions with Maven's rules instead of guessing

`Scheme` had no Maven arm, so `pkg:maven/...` components fell to `Infer`,
where a Maven qualifier is read as either a Debian revision or a semver
pre-release depending on its spelling. `1.0-SNAPSHOT` parses as
`Version::Deb` and `1.0` as `Version::Semver`, and a mixed pair is `None`,
so `--fail-on version-downgrade` could not see a snapshot-vs-release change
at all. Where both sides did land on `Deb`, the verdict could be backwards:
dpkg orders revisions bytewise, so `1.0-Final -> 1.0-SNAPSHOT` (a real
downgrade) passed and `1.0-SNAPSHOT -> 1.0-Final` (the release) failed the
gate. `_` is outside the Debian alphabet, so a JDK spelling like `1.7.0_80`
was opaque on top of that.

Adds `Version::Maven` and `maven_cmp`, implementing the version-order
specification published at maven.apache.org/pom.html: tokens split on `.`,
`-`, `_` and digit/character transitions, trailing null tokens trimmed at
the end and before each remaining hyphen, and the qualifier ranking
alpha < beta < milestone < rc = cr < snapshot < final = ga = release < sp,
with unrecognized qualifiers lexically above all of them. `parse_lenient`
is untouched: the variant is only reachable through `parse_for_ecosystem`,
so every existing signature and result stands.

Two points where the published prose is not self-consistent are resolved
in favour of the ordering being a total order, which is also what Maven's
own `ComparableVersion` does:

- the prose says a padded null "depends on the separator of the other
  version". It has to depend on the *kind* of the token it faces instead:
  under the separator rule `1 > 1.foo` (padded to `1.0`) but `1 < 1-foo`
  (padded to `1-""`), while the spec's own examples fix `1.foo = 1-foo`.
  `IntItem.compareTo(null)`/`StringItem.compareTo(null)` pad by kind.
- the prose renders the cross-separator rule as
  `.qualifier = -qualifier < -number < .number`. Read as "any dot-qualifier
  equals any hyphen-qualifier" that makes `1.foo = 1-bar` while
  `1-bar < 1-foo`, so the separator is ignored for qualifiers and ranks
  only numbers.

`maven_ordering_is_a_total_order` pins both; it fails on either reading.

* order Maven versions with ComparableVersion's nested list model

the flat token model got the dotted qualifier form wrong: 1.0.0.CR1 kept
the two null tokens 1.0.0-RC1 dropped, so the spelling Spring, JBoss,
Hibernate and Netty publish sorted as a separate ladder from the
hyphenated one, and 1.0.0.CR1 -> 1.0.0-CR2 failed --fail-on
version-downgrade on a genuine upgrade.

folding a qualifier's separator to a hyphen fixes that shape but breaks
another: ComparableVersion opens a sub-list for a qualifier reached past
an item, and a sub-list outranks a bare qualifier, so 1-0.alpha is
greater than 1-alpha, not equal to it. depth is not expressible in a
flat token sequence, so parse to the item tree ComparableVersion builds
instead: `.`, `-` and `_` split, every separator but `.` opens a
sub-list, as does a qualifier reached from a digit or introduced by a
`.` after an item, and each list drops its trailing nulls.

validated against the real ComparableVersion (apache/maven maven-3.9.x)
run under java: 0 divergences over 47,089 pairs drawn from Maven's own
ComparableVersionTest literals plus JDK, Spring, JBoss, Hibernate and
Netty coordinates. the flat model was 1,220 wrong on the same set.

`_` stays a separator, the spec reading, unchanged from the previous
commit and still deliberate.

* bound the Maven item tree's nesting depth

the item tree nests one level per `-`/`_` separator and per digit/letter
transition, and maven_list_cmp/maven_item_cmp recurse once per level, so a
version string from an untrusted SBOM could drive the process into a stack
overflow (SIGABRT, rc 134) that main does not have.

maven_parse now declines past 64 levels and parse_maven declines with it, so
such a version stays Opaque and the pair is skipped rather than force-ordered
-- the same policy already applied to codenames and git hashes. capping in the
parser rather than making the comparator iterative also keeps the deep tree
from ever being built, which matters because dropping one recurses too.

reproduced through the shipped CLI before the fix at 40,000 separators
(160 KB CycloneDX file, debug build) and, separately, at 40,000 digit/letter
transitions with no separator at all -- both rc 134, both rc 0 now.

the cap is roughly nine times the deepest realistic coordinate: the worst of
`1.7.0_80-b15`, `4.1.86.Final`, `1.0-alpha-1-SNAPSHOT-20240101.123456-7` and
friends bounds at 7. every documented vector in the Maven tests parses under
it, which the tests enforce -- their helper panics on a declined pair.

maven_ordering_is_a_total_order is renamed to what it pins: the ordering is
not a total order, and neither is ComparableVersion.

licenses on the declared SPDX expression, not a flat identifier set (#123)

* gate licenses on the declared SPDX expression, not a flat identifier set

parse_license_expression kept only expr.requirements()' license ids and
discarded the operators, so every license gate read its input with the wrong
semantics: "MIT OR GPL-3.0-only" and "MIT AND GPL-3.0-only" both flattened to
{GPL-3.0-only, MIT}, and "GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0" was
indistinguishable from bare "GPL-2.0-only". that over-fired --deny-license and
--fail-on copyleft-added on choices a policy would permit, reported
allow-list violations for expressions satisfiable inside the allow-list, and
made a component silently losing a GPL linking exception invisible to the diff.

Component now carries the declared expression alongside the flattened set,
populated by both ingesters, and the gates evaluate it with
spdx::Expression::evaluate: a deny fires only when no satisfying choice avoids
a denied license, an allow only when no satisfying choice lies inside the
allow-list, and copyleft-added only when the new expression cannot be satisfied
without a copyleft license the old one did not already force. an expression
change that leaves the identifier set alone surfaces as
FieldChange::LicenseExpression so the exception loss is both visible and
gateable. components with no declared expression — free text, LicenseRef-, or
per-license id/name entries — keep exactly the previous flat-set behaviour.

* compare licensings by what satisfies them, not by expression spelling

the differ asked `expressions_equivalent`, which answered `true` whenever one
side declared no expression. `Licensing::satisfiable` reads an absent
expression as a conjunction of the identifier set, so the two surfaces
disagreed: `MIT OR GPL-3.0-only` collapsing into a bare `{MIT, GPL-3.0-only}`
pair went from exit 0 to exit 2 under `--deny-license gpl-3.0-only` while the
diff called it `Unchanged: 1`, and both `--fail-on copyleft-added` and
`--fail-on license-changed` stayed quiet.

both ends of the predicate are now decided by the same rule: two licensings
differ exactly when different sets of licenses satisfy them. `Licensing`
expands into its minimal satisfying requirement sets and those are compared,
so a side with no expression is the conjunction of its identifiers and matches
an expression that means the same thing. that closes the loose end and also
the strict one the reviewer paired with it — operand order stops being a
change, which is a behaviour change from the previous commit's documented
choice, since `GPL-3.0-only OR MIT` offers the consumer exactly what
`MIT OR GPL-3.0-only` does.

expansion is capped at 64 alternatives; past that the two expressions are
compared as parse trees, which is what `main` did, and a capped expression
never matches a bare identifier set.

* compare copyleft burdens per satisfying choice, not per license

mandatory_copyleft tests each copyleft license individually, so under a
choice between copyleft licenses no single one is unavoidable and the old
side's burden reads as empty. copyleft_obligations_added then asks whether
the new side can be satisfied copyleft-free, fails, and reports every
copyleft it mentions -- firing when the copyleft choice is unchanged and
only a permissive operand moved, which main is quiet about.

reduce each side's choices() to the copyleft each one carries, keep the
minimal ones, and fire only when no option the new side offers is a subset
of an option the old side offered, reporting the union of the minimal new
burdens minus what every old option already forced. that also stops the
report naming copyleft the consumer can avoid: MIT -> GPL-3.0-only AND
(MPL-2.0 OR ISC) now names GPL-3.0-only alone.

past the 64-alternative cap choices() is None, so the previous rule stays
as the fallback; README and the changelog gain the matching caveat on the
operand-order rule, which the doc comment already carried.

* say the copyleft-added report is a union across choices

README and the changelog claimed the report names "only the licenses no
satisfying choice avoids". that holds when the new side's minimal burdens
are nested -- the MPL-2.0 OR ISC shape -- but not when they are
incomparable, because copyleft_obligations_added reports the union across
them. against the built binary:

  MIT -> GPL-2.0-only OR AGPL-3.0-only
    AGPL-3.0-only, GPL-2.0-only, though a consumer takes one or the other
  MIT -> (GPL-3.0-only AND MPL-2.0) OR (AGPL-3.0-only AND EPL-2.0)
    AGPL-3.0-only, GPL-3.0-only, MPL-2.0, and the AGPL branch avoids MPL-2.0

the verdict is right in both -- copyleft really is introduced -- and
naming every license the consumer might end up under is the useful
warning, so only the claim about the list changes. the rustdoc on the
public function carried the same overclaim and is corrected with it.

test_copyleft_obligations_added_names_only_the_unavoidable_licenses was
likewise named for a property neither of its cases tested; it is renamed
and gains both incomparable shapes. reporting the intersection instead of
the union -- the behaviour the old wording described -- passes its two

discarded the operators, so every license gate read its input with the wrong
semantics: "MIT OR GPL-3.0-only" and "MIT AND GPL-3.0-only" both flattened to
{GPL-3.0-only, MIT}, and "GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0" was
indistinguishable from bare "GPL-2.0-only". that over-fired --deny-license and
--fail-on copyleft-added on choices a policy would permit, reported
allow-list violations for expressions satisfiable inside the allow-list, and
made a component silently losing a GPL linking exception invisible to the diff.

Component now carries the declared expression alongside the flattened set,
populated by both ingesters, and the gates evaluate it with
spdx::Expression::evaluate: a deny fires only when no satisfying choice avoids
a denied license, an allow only when no satisfying choice lies inside the
allow-list, and copyleft-added only when the new expression cannot be satisfied
without a copyleft license the old one did not already force. an expression
change that leaves the identifier set alone surfaces as
FieldChange::LicenseExpression so the exception loss is both visible and
gateable. components with no declared expression — free text, LicenseRef-, or
per-license id/name entries — keep exactly the previous flat-set behaviour.

* compare licensings by what satisfies them, not by expression spelling

the differ asked `expressions_equivalent`, which answered `true` whenever one
side declared no expression. `Licensing::satisfiable` reads an absent
expression as a conjunction of the identifier set, so the two surfaces
disagreed: `MIT OR GPL-3.0-only` collapsing into a bare `{MIT, GPL-3.0-only}`
pair went from exit 0 to exit 2 under `--deny-license gpl-3.0-only` while the
diff called it `Unchanged: 1`, and both `--fail-on copyleft-added` and
`--fail-on license-changed` stayed quiet.

both ends of the predicate are now decided by the same rule: two licensings
differ exactly when different sets of licenses satisfy them. `Licensing`
expands into its minimal satisfying requirement sets and those are compared,
so a side with no expression is the conjunction of its identifiers and matches
an expression that means the same thing. that closes the loose end and also
the strict one the reviewer paired with it — operand order stops being a
change, which is a behaviour change from the previous commit's documented
choice, since `GPL-3.0-only OR MIT` offers the consumer exactly what
`MIT OR GPL-3.0-only` does.

expansion is capped at 64 alternatives; past that the two expressions are
compared as parse trees, which is what `main` did, and a capped expression
never matches a bare identifier set.

* compare copyleft burdens per satisfying choice, not per license

mandatory_copyleft tests each copyleft license individually, so under a
choice between copyleft licenses no single one is unavoidable and the old
side's burden reads as empty. copyleft_obligations_added then asks whether
the new side can be satisfied copyleft-free, fails, and reports every
copyleft it mentions -- firing when the copyleft choice is unchanged and
only a permissive operand moved, which main is quiet about.

minimal ones, and fire only when no option the new side offers is a subset

burdens minus what every old option already forced. that also stops the

past the 64-alternative cap choices() is None, so the previous rule stays
as the fallback; README and the changelog gain the matching caveat on the
operand-order rule, which the doc comment already carried.

RPM versions with rpmvercmp instead of dpkg rules (#122)

* order RPM versions with rpmvercmp instead of dpkg rules

`Scheme` had no RPM arm, so `pkg:rpm/...` components fell to `Infer` and
were ordered with Debian's `verrevcmp` while three doc comments claimed
RPM was covered. The two algorithms return opposite verdicts on ordinary
inputs — dpkg ranks an alpha segment above a numeric one, rpm below it —
so `--fail-on version-downgrade` could fire on an upgrade, and neither
`_` nor `^` is in the Debian version alphabet at all, leaving stock RHEL
release strings like `4.4.2-2.el7_9` uncomparable.

Adds `Version::Rpm` and `rpmvercmp`, transcribed from rpm's
`lib/rpmvercmp.c` including the 4.15+ `^` arm, wired to the `rpm` purl
type. `parse_lenient` is untouched: the new variant is only reachable
through `parse_for_ecosystem`, so every existing signature and result
stands. Deletes the false RPM claims from the `Deb`, `verrevcmp`,
`parse_deb`, `is_deb_char`, `deb_cmp` and module docs.

* reframe the RPM changelog entry around the silent skip

the entry copied the shape of the two above it and led with a
mis-ordering, which is the narrower of the two failures. an rpm
component never reached Scheme::Deb: it fell through to Infer, where
`4.4.2-2.el7_9` parses as Opaque because `_` is outside the Debian
alphabet, the pair compares None, and the gate exits 0 on a real
downgrade.

both halves are real. over a 163-string corpus of RPM spellings
(26,569 pairs), 13,117 were skipped by the old path and ordered by the
new one; 1,070 were ordered both ways with opposite verdicts. the
reversal needs both sides to land on Deb, which the epoch and `~`
spellings do (`1:1.a -> 1:1.0`) but `1.a -> 1.1` does not — `1.1`
reads as semver and a mixed pair is None, so that pair was skipped
too.

* restore the two upstream non-ASCII rpmvercmp vectors

the table claims to be rpm's tests/rpmvercmp.at transcribed, but
upstream's `1.1.α` vs `1.1.ββ` and `1.1.ββ` vs `1.1.αα` had been
written with α on both sides. the expectations were right — every row
in that block collapses to `1.1.` plus separators — but the second
substitute was a self-comparison, which rpmvercmp short-circuits on its
first line, so it exercised nothing.

the wildcard identity fallback by version (#116)

* align the wildcard identity fallback by version

phase 2a pairs exact (ecosystem, name) buckets through align_by_version,
but the two wildcard cases still popped an arbitrary old id per new
component. diffing the same dependency set across serialization formats
therefore cross-paired version lines: an npm SBOM re-exported without
purls parses to ecosystem None, so libfoo 1.0.0/2.0.0 came back as
1.0.0 -> 2.0.0 plus a 2.0.0 -> 1.0.0 downgrade, and --fail-on
version-downgrade exited 3 on a pure format change.

both cases now collect their candidate bucket and run it through
align_by_version like 2a does, draining the consumed old ids. an
ecosystem-less new component pools every old ecosystem carrying that
name into one candidate set, so the version-nearest old component wins
rather than the alphabetically first; exact matches still resolve first
in 2a, so an exact-ecosystem pairing keeps precedence over a wildcard
one even when the wildcard candidate is version-nearer.

the per-component case-1 lookup is dropped: 2a pairs min(old, new) for
every exact bucket, so by the time 2b runs one side of that bucket is
always empty and the lookup can no longer match.

* trim the wildcard reconciliation changelog entry

the bullet ran 591 characters against a 233-359 range for the other
Unreleased entries, and its second sentence documented the internal
tie-break rule (version-nearest candidate wins over alphabetically
first) rather than user-visible behaviour. dropped that sentence and
tightened the first clause to 357 characters; the fix, the concrete
cross-format symptom and the affected --fail-on gate all survive.

no source or test changes.

align the wildcard identity fallback by version (#116)

* align the wildcard identity fallback by version

phase 2a pairs exact (ecosystem, name) buckets through align_by_version,
but the two wildcard cases still popped an arbitrary old id per new
component. diffing the same dependency set across serialization formats
therefore cross-paired version lines: an npm SBOM re-exported without
purls parses to ecosystem None, so libfoo 1.0.0/2.0.0 came back as
1.0.0 -> 2.0.0 plus a 2.0.0 -> 1.0.0 downgrade, and --fail-on
version-downgrade exited 3 on a pure format change.

both cases now collect their candidate bucket and run it through
align_by_version like 2a does, draining the consumed old ids. an
ecosystem-less new component pools every old ecosystem carrying that
name into one candidate set, so the version-nearest old component wins
rather than the alphabetically first; exact matches still resolve first
in 2a, so an exact-ecosystem pairing keeps precedence over a wildcard
one even when the wildcard candidate is version-nearer.

the per-component case-1 lookup is dropped: 2a pairs min(old, new) for
every exact bucket, so by the time 2b runs one side of that bucket is
always empty and the lookup can no longer match.

* trim the wildcard reconciliation changelog entry

the bullet ran 591 characters against a 233-359 range for the other
Unreleased entries, and its second sentence documented the internal
tie-break rule (version-nearest candidate wins over alphabetically
first) rather than user-visible behaviour. dropped that sentence and
tightened the first clause to 357 characters; the fix, the concrete
cross-format symptom and the affected --fail-on gate all survive.
